title: Allele Frequency
objectives: Calculate allele frequencies from genotype counts.
Distinguish a genome, gene pool and population.
State Hardy–Weinberg assumptions and predictions.

glossary.definition: The proportion of all allele copies at a defined locus represented by one allele.
All alleles present in a reproducing population.
A model in which allele and genotype frequencies remain constant under specified conditions.

slides.title: Define the population first
slides.html: A population is a group whose members reproduce with one another within a defined setting. A study must specify its boundaries, sampling time and locus. Two samples from different places need not represent the same breeding population. Frequencies describe that defined population, rather than every person carrying the same species name.

slides.title: Count allele copies, not visible traits
slides.html: At an autosomal locus in a diploid population, each person normally contributes two allele copies. An AA person contributes two A copies; an Aa person contributes one A and one a. Dominance affects the phenotype but does not change this accounting. A recessive allele can be common without being visibly expressed in most people.

diagram.caption: Each row represents a diploid genotype at one locus, not a whole chromosome. Count both copies.

slides.title: A worked frequency calculation
slides.html: Suppose 100 people include 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa individuals. There are 200 allele copies. A contributes 72 + 48 = 120 copies, so its frequency is 120/200 = 0.60. The a frequency is 0.40. These calculations use observed counts and do not require Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

slides.title: Genotype frequency is a different measure
slides.html: In the same example, the genotype frequencies are 0.36 AA, 0.48 Aa and 0.16 aa. Each denominator is 100 people, rather than 200 allele copies. If A is completely dominant, the A-associated phenotype frequency is 0.84, because AA and Aa contribute. That phenotype frequency is not the A allele frequency.

slides.title: Genomes and gene pools
slides.html: A genome is the complete genetic material of an organism, including coding and non-coding DNA. A gene pool is a population-level collection of alleles. Genomics compares or analyses genomes. The terms therefore refer to different scales: a person has a genome, while a defined reproducing population has a gene pool.

slides.title: The Hardy–Weinberg reference model
slides.html: For a two-allele autosomal locus, write p for the A frequency and q for the a frequency. Then p + q = 1. With random union of gametes, expected genotype frequencies are p² for AA, 2pq for Aa and q² for aa. The two heterozygote combinations explain the factor of two.

diagram.caption: Expected values under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model; this is not evidence that every population meets the assumptions.

slides.title: Conditions for equilibrium
slides.html: The model assumes a very large population, random mating with respect to the locus, no migration, no mutation and no natural selection at that locus. Large population size minimises random sampling effects. Real populations may approximate some conditions while violating others. Non-random mating alone can change genotype proportions without necessarily changing allele frequencies.

slides.title: Using the model carefully
slides.html: If the observed recessive phenotype frequency is 0.09 and aa alone produces it, equilibrium gives q² = 0.09, q = 0.30 and p = 0.70. Expected heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.42. Inferring carrier frequency this way requires the inheritance and equilibrium assumptions; phenotype counts alone do not establish them.

slides.title: An allele-frequency denominator is locus-specific
slides.html: For a typical autosomal locus in a diploid sample of N individuals, the denominator is 2N allele copies. This rule assumes each sampled individual contributes two copies of the locus. Other situations, such as a sex-linked locus or a copy-number change, require different accounting. State the locus and sampling assumptions rather than automatically multiplying every biological count by two. Frequency is a proportion and can be expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage.

slides.title: Worked example from observed genotypes
slides.html: A hypothetical sample contains 40 AA, 45 Aa and 15 aa individuals. There are 200 allele copies. The A count is twice 40 plus 45, giving 125; A frequency is 125/200 = 0.625. The a count is 45 plus twice 15, giving 75; a frequency is 0.375. Adding these frequencies gives one, which provides a useful arithmetic check for a two-allele locus.

slides.title: Compare the same measure across samples
slides.html: Suppose a later sample of 100 individuals contains 50 AA, 40 Aa and 10 aa. Its A frequency is (100 + 40)/200 = 0.70. Compared with 0.625, the increase is 0.075, or 7.5 percentage points. The relative percentage increase is 0.075/0.625 × 100 = 12%. These are different descriptions. Neither establishes that natural selection was the cause without additional evidence about sampling and evolutionary mechanisms.

slides.title: Why a small sample can mislead
slides.html: A sample is not necessarily the entire breeding population. Random sampling variation can produce different observed frequencies even when the underlying population frequency is unchanged. Samples taken from different subgroups can also differ because of how the population was defined. Larger representative samples generally improve precision, but increasing the size of a biased sample does not remove its bias. Repeated, comparable sampling helps distinguish measurement limitations from evidence of biological change.

slides.title: A three-allele example uses the same principle
slides.html: At a hypothetical locus with three alleles, A, B and C, all copies still belong in the denominator. If there are 30 A copies, 50 B copies and 20 C copies, the total is 100 and the frequencies are 0.30, 0.50 and 0.20. The frequencies sum to one. A formula written only as p + q = 1 is specific to the two-allele example, not a universal limit on allele number.

slides.title: Hardy–Weinberg is a reference, not a measurement
slides.html: Observed genotype counts allow direct calculation of allele frequency without assuming equilibrium. Hardy–Weinberg expectations instead use allele frequencies and random union of gametes to predict genotype proportions under stated conditions. A discrepancy between observed and expected proportions does not uniquely identify its cause. Population structure, non-random mating, sampling variation and several evolutionary processes can affect the comparison. Treat this as supporting modelling rather than a shortcut that replaces actual observations.

slides.title: A frequency change needs a causal explanation
slides.html: To explain a population change, link a mechanism to allele transmission across generations. Mutation introduces new variants, migration with reproduction connects populations, drift changes representation through chance, and selection changes contributions associated with heritable phenotypes. Multiple mechanisms can operate together. A graph can demonstrate a trend in the measured frequency while leaving its cause unresolved. A strong response separates the numerical trend from the biological evidence used to explain it.

title: Gene Flow
objectives: Explain when movement becomes gene flow.
Calculate a mixed population allele frequency.
Relate barriers and gene flow to population divergence.

glossary.definition: Transfer of alleles between populations through successful reproduction.
Movement of individuals; it causes gene flow only when alleles enter a breeding population.
Separation that reduces opportunities for reproduction between populations.

slides.title: Alleles move between populations
slides.html: Gene flow occurs when individuals or gametes from one population contribute alleles to another population’s next generation. It connects gene pools that would otherwise change more independently. Movement alone is not sufficient: a visitor who produces no offspring in the receiving population has not transferred alleles into its breeding gene pool.

slides.title: Reproduction is the connecting step
slides.html: A person can contribute alleles to another population without permanently moving there. Conversely, permanent migration need not cause gene flow if no reproduction follows. This distinction is important when interpreting travel records. The biological process concerns inherited contributions across generations, rather than nationality, residence or the act of crossing a boundary.

diagram.caption: A simplified mechanism: the connecting steps are explained in the accompanying text.

slides.title: Mixing changes frequencies
slides.html: Consider a simplified pool of 20 allele copies, of which 4 are A. A second contributing group brings 10 copies, of which 6 are A. The combined pool contains 10 A copies among 30 copies, giving 0.333. Weighting by the number of copies matters; averaging 0.20 and 0.60 without weights would be incorrect.

diagram.caption: Illustrative allele copies at one locus: coloured dots represent A. These are not counts of people or measured historical data.

slides.title: Gene flow can increase local variation
slides.html: An arriving allele absent from the receiving population adds a genetic variant locally. This does not mean migration creates that allele: mutation originally generated the sequence variation. Gene flow transports existing variation. Its effect depends on which alleles arrive, how many descendants receive them and the size of the receiving population.

slides.title: Connections can reduce differences
slides.html: Repeated exchange often makes allele frequencies in connected populations more similar. If both populations contribute offspring across their boundary, differences produced by drift or local selection can be reduced. Gene flow does not guarantee identical populations. Strong selection in different environments may maintain differences despite some exchange of alleles.

slides.title: Barriers are biological and social
slides.html: Oceans, deserts and mountain ranges can reduce contact, depending on the mobility of the species. In humans, distance, transport, settlement patterns and partner choice can affect reproductive connections. These are influences on gene flow, not absolute labels. Populations may have partial connections, and the strength of a barrier can change over time.

slides.title: Gene flow and local adaptation
slides.html: An allele favoured in one environment may be less favourable elsewhere. Incoming alleles can therefore assist adaptation, have little effect, or oppose local selection. The outcome depends on both migration and reproductive success. It is inaccurate to describe every incoming allele as beneficial, harmful or automatically selected into the population.

slides.title: Connection and divergence
slides.html: Reduced gene flow allows populations to accumulate differences through mutation, drift and selection. Continued gene flow can oppose this divergence. However, a geographical barrier does not automatically produce a new species. Reproductive isolation must develop and persist; the processes and time required differ among organisms and circumstances.

slides.title: Movement is measured through inherited contribution
slides.html: For gene flow, the important event is transfer of alleles into another population through reproduction. A person who travels but contributes no gametes to the next generation has not produced that genetic effect. Conversely, alleles can enter a population through reproduction without permanent relocation. A migration count is therefore a demographic observation, while gene flow is an inherited contribution. The two measures can be related without being interchangeable.

slides.title: A weighted mixing model states its assumptions
slides.html: Consider an illustrative receiving pool containing 160 allele copies, including 32 A copies, so A frequency is 0.20. A contributing group adds 40 copies, including 24 A copies, so its A frequency is 0.60. If those contributions are combined directly in the model, the new pool contains 56 A copies among 200, giving 0.28. The arithmetic weights each source by its copy count rather than averaging the two frequencies equally.

slides.title: The same migrants affect smaller pools more
slides.html: If the same 40 contributing copies instead join a receiving pool of 40 copies containing 8 A copies, the combined frequency is (8 + 24)/(40 + 40) = 0.40. The receiving frequency began at 0.20 in both examples, but the change is greater in the smaller receiving pool. The outcome therefore depends on the migrants’ proportional genetic contribution, not only their number or their initial allele frequency.

slides.title: Not all arriving alleles contribute equally
slides.html: The weighted model assumes specified allele contributions to the pooled population. In a real population, the reproductive success of migrants and their descendants can vary. Some incoming alleles may be lost by chance or selected against, while others persist or increase. A count of arrivals is not enough to predict the frequency several generations later. Separate the initial transfer from the subsequent effects of mating patterns, drift and selection.

slides.title: A barrier can reduce rather than eliminate connection
slides.html: Geographical distance, habitat discontinuity and patterns of partner choice can reduce the probability of reproduction between groups. The barrier need not be complete. Occasional inherited contributions can still connect gene pools even when most reproduction occurs locally. The strength of the barrier can also change over time. Describing a barrier as partial is more biologically informative than assuming that two populations are completely isolated simply because they occupy different places.

slides.title: Gene flow interacts with local selection
slides.html: If different environments favour different heritable phenotypes, local selection can maintain differences despite some exchange of alleles. Strong exchange can also reduce differences that drift or selection would otherwise produce. The balance depends on the rate of genetic contribution and the reproductive effects of the alleles in each environment. Gene flow is therefore not automatically beneficial or harmful, and connected populations do not necessarily become genetically identical.

slides.title: Evidence for connection requires careful comparison
slides.html: A shared allele in two populations is consistent with gene flow but can also reflect shared ancestry. To distinguish explanations, researchers can compare multiple sequence regions, their distribution and the timing and direction suggested by additional evidence. Small or unrepresentative samples can miss rare variants. A defensible conclusion states what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain, without treating genetic population boundaries as fixed social categories or implying a biological hierarchy among people.
